The Long-Tail Bank
AnswerSimulatorWhat flips itEvidenceSupplierMethod

Sami Hecheime · Independent research, not investment advice; no affiliation with any firm named. Status 24 Oct 2026.

Can a wealth bank earn more by selling many small niche products next to its AI-led core, on one shared platform? I built a model bank and tested it against three US banks’ public figures and 29 pre-registered tests.

Yes at Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs*, in the model.*Goldman Sachs on its principal cash measure: at least 88% of simulated worlds. On the prudent cash estimate set by the rule: 61%.

The general pre-registered test (H12) was not supported: 55% of simulated worlds, bar 75%. Not supported

Amazon next to Walmart: niches sold beside the AI-led core, with shared logistics as the engine. The long-tail bank (“Amazon model”) wins at least 75% of simulated worlds if its platform costs at most 0.164% (model output) of client assets, or if client cash is at least 2.97% (model output). Either one alone is enough.

    Try a setting

      The rule of thumb

      unknownPlatform at most 0.164% (model output)
      unknownClient cash at least 2.972% (model output)
      never aloneDemand: at most 66% (model output) of worlds, even at 30%bar 75%

      Either of the first two is enough for 75% of worlds, each fixed alone with the others drawn (step 13, 28 Sep–4 Oct 2026). Their intervals: platform 0.158–0.170% (model output), cash 2.93–3.02% (model output). “Within margin” means inside that interval.

      Where the lead comes from

      Central case over 20 years, discounted at 8%. Unknown inputs sit at central values: platform 0.30%, cash 2%, demand 20%. The niche gain leans on a platform cost counted once (note 2).

      A simulated world is one draw of markets and of the inputs nobody knows. Values come from the R model, precomputed on a grid and interpolated between grid points; each share carries its Monte Carlo margin. A named bank starts at 20% demand, as in the headline figure: an assumption, not a measure.

      Break-even at the central case: platform 0.375% (model output), cash 1.62% (model output), demand 12.0% (model output).

      The gain from adding niches leans on a fixed platform cost counted once, a modelling assumption. Client switching between banks is assumed (25–75% of niche-seeking clients) and measured nowhere.

      The field always draws 10,000 dots, whatever the cell’s sample size, so each dot is one ten-thousandth of the worlds. Won worlds fill column by column from the left, top to bottom, so the edge between blue and pale sits exactly on the share; lighter dots on either side of it are within the 95% Monte Carlo margin.

      Note 3About the three inputsUnits, grid ranges, and what the 27% demand survey measures

      Platform start-up cost. Percent of client assets, paid once; a yearly running cost follows the official path. The control steps through the grid’s real nodes, 0.10% to 0.60%, plus two added points: the robust threshold (0.164% (model output)) and Morgan Stanley’s measured platform price (0.1654%).

      Client cash held today. Percent of client assets held as client cash at the bank. The model pools it into a smaller shared cushion. The pre-registered grid covers 1–4%.

      Clients wanting niches. Measured intention: 27% of Schwab ETF investors planned to buy thematic ETFs (2023; 23.5% in 2024, 31% in 2025). That is retail intention, not private-bank clients, and AI themes are included. Letter of the rule: partly met; retained 4 Oct: met.

      AI scenario. AI-led stocks move once, in year 2. “All four” pools the four scenarios, as the official grid did.

      Note 4Shared logistics, in detailWholesale routing, the cushion in an AI fall, and an exploratory routing rule

      52% (model output) of niche market orders take the wholesale route. The main gain is the pooled cash cushion: 2% per client becomes 1.04% (model output) pooled, worth about 4.6 bp (model output) a year; the interest income on that cash is not counted.

      Logistics alone, with no niches, loses $1.27bn (model output) (control bank minus traditional bank). An exploratory order-routing rule reached +$1.18bn (model output) in 58.6% (model output) of worlds; it was chosen after seeing the result and is not evidence (step 8bis, 26 Sep 2026).

      An illustrative client in an AI fall

      A 20% niche pocket lost 2.3 pp (model output) less when tech fell 40% [0.0–5.2 (model output)]. On real ETFs in 2011–2026 it cost 1.28 pp a year. A shock absorber, not a shield.

      That cost is H8, officialInconclusive

      Median 12-month loss, illustrative client, model; cushion shown when the 90% interval lies above zero

      When the pocket pays for itself

      Tool 15 asks how likely a 40% AI crash must be, each year, before the pocket’s cost is worth paying. The project estimates no crash probability; this is a model decision tool, not advice.

      12% (model output)a year, for a typical illustrative client (11–18% across five risk profiles), 40% crash 4.5% (model output)a year, for a 60% crash
      Note 7The client stress test and tool 15Step 7h, a long-history reference, and the guardrails checked on 1939–2026

      Step 7h stress test, “as today” variant, AI-era data, median 12-month loss of an illustrative client; niches are French industries. Price: H8, real ETFs Apr 2011–Jul 2026, −1.28 pp a year [−2.10, −0.12].

      Long-history reference, not AI-era: tech fell 40% or more within 12 months in 2.7% of 12-month windows (1927–2026). At that frequency the best pocket is 0%.

      Guardrails in the model: tech never above its market weight, a loss limit, turnover at most 10% a month, and a storm rule. 0 violations of the tech and storm rules, and the loss limit held in 50 of 50 cases; the turnover cap was exceeded 5 times, each forced by the tech rule (check on 1939–2026, long history).

      Holders, not dollars

      On Robinhood in summer 2019, the tail held little of the money and many of the holdings. So did the AI-led head.

      Niche ETFs: 5.7% of ETF dollars → 17.6% of Robinhood holdings. AI-led head: 3.0% → 14.8%.

      Note 9Why two verdictsThe dry run raised 77 false alarms in 1,000 against a cap of 75

      In the dry run on fictitious panels, the worst null family raised 77 false alarms in 1,000 (7.7%) against a cap of 75 (7.5%). The pre-registered text forbids using the Monte Carlo margin in the thesis’s favour, so the official verdict was inconclusive before launch.

      The retained rule, fixed on 21 Oct before launch and before any client value was seen, but after a trial dry run with the same seeds had shown 77 of 1,000, passes when the lower bound of that margin is at or below 7.5%.

      Dry-run power at 2×: 0.846. Chance of passing with no effect: 0 in 1,000 under both rules.

      Note 10Caveats written before the resultSeven, from attention-driven buying to missing archive files
      • Exposure, not access; holders, not dollars; one app, one quarter, before the AI era.
      • No measure of bank profit, money placed or clients’ other holdings.
      • The head (AI-led and broad-index ETFs) also had more holders: 2.93× (p = 0.0007), against a prediction of at most 1×.
      • Niche holder growth did not shift measurably when other brokers went commission-free in Oct 2019 (β −0.014, p = 0.12).
      • The direction was partly published before (Ben-David et al., 2023). Attention-driven Robinhood buying is followed by −4.7% over 20 days (Barber et al., 2022); specialised ETFs lose about 30% over five years, risk-adjusted (Ben-David et al., 2023).
      • No archive file does not mean not on the app; 126 series had no summer-2019 file.
      • Low-price reading (declared before launch, own script, not a trial, no effect on either verdict): 3.93× [2.47–6.34] in the two cheapest price fifths; the interval contains 3, and the 3× bar applies to the estimate. Its 3× bar was chosen on 23 Oct knowing its power (0.62 at 2×, 0.91 at 3×), after the blindness incident. Source: Bloomberg (price fields, no values shown).

      The thesis in four pieces

      A bank sells many small niche products next to the head (AI-led funds and broad indices) on one shared platform. Each piece uses its own data and its own meaning of “niche”, so results do not chain directly (note 8).

      1

      Size

      Does the tail weigh enough once added up?

      Niches hold 4.08% of US equity-ETF assets [2.66–6.04]; the bar was 5%.

      H19Not supportedretained Partly supported · 18 Oct, after launch
      H19-PCprivate credit, pending, Dec 2026
      2

      Money

      Does the tail earn more per dollar?

      Niche ETFs charge 2.1× the average fee per dollar [1.62–2.79]. Issuer revenue, not margin; their investors earned less.

      H20Partly supportedretained Supported · 18 Oct, after launch
      H20-BlackRockNot testable
      H20-PCprivate credit, pending, about 9–10 Nov
      3

      Access

      Does easy access go with more holders or money in the tail?

      Niche ETFs had 3.32× the Robinhood holders of same-size, same-issuer ETFs; the head also had 2.93×. Exposure, not access. One app, one quarter (Robinhood, summer 2019). Money moving when trading became free (H21, Oct 2019) had power 0.14.

      H22Inconclusiveretained Supported · rule fixed 21 Oct, before launch, after a trial dry run showed 7.7%
      H21Not testable
      H23pending, Nov · H24 to be pre-registered
      4

      Logistics

      Does putting head and niches together save liquidity?

      In the bank simulation the long-tail bank wins 55% (model output) of worlds; the bar was 75%. Niches on an existing shared platform add +$2.12bn (model output), positive in 100% (model output) of worlds.

      In private credit, all 7 counted trials failed (H16b–H18).

      Pending and dated forecasts

      The view from a platform supplier

      BlackRock as the example. It is not a bank in this model: it sells the catalogue (iShares, managed accounts) and Aladdin Wealth, and the banks are possible clients.

      A hypothetical platform at a known price

      At J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs the input the model lacks is the platform price: 55ip (J.P. Morgan, 2020) and Folio (Goldman Sachs, 2020) were bought at prices never published. Share of simulated worlds won with each bank’s cash figure and 20% demand. No bank has bought a platform at that price.

      R model, exact 10,000-world presets, 8% discount, 20 years. 0.10% is the model’s floor; the project does not extrapolate below it. J.P. Morgan cash is an estimate; Goldman Sachs uses the prudent estimate.

      Selling the platform

      At the robust ceiling, a platform sold to the $500bn model bank would bring $0.82bn (model output) upfront plus an assumed $66m (model output) a year: about $2.1bn (model output) over 20 years, undiscounted gross revenue. That is 1.7–2.5× (model output) the extra iShares fees of the bank’s niche pocket (demand 30% to 20%); the fees are a ceiling, since the whole pocket is assumed to sit in iShares. Model arithmetic, step 13h.

      Price benchmark: Aperio

      BlackRock paid $1.05bn in cash for Aperio (2020). Divided by each bank’s client assets, that is 0.013% (Morgan Stanley), 0.027% (J.P. Morgan) and 0.053% (Goldman Sachs), all below the 0.164% robust ceiling. It is indicative and cannot fail: an acquisition multiple (2.9% of Aperio’s own $36bn), not a platform cost.

      Sources: BlackRock release of 23 Nov 2020 and 10-K 2021 (Aperio price); the three banks’ 2Q-2026 filings (client assets).

      Fees per dollar at iShares

      3.3×0.382% a year for sector and thematic niches against 0.116% for core equity ETFs, across 257 iShares equity ETFs

      A measurement, not a test. A prediction I wrote before measuring (at least 5× core) was false.

      Source: Bloomberg (capitalisations, 2 Oct 2023); fees: public iShares product list (1 Sep 2026). Step 13h, 6 Oct 2026.

      Note 14What Aladdin Wealth is and is notIt builds portfolios; it does not net orders or pool client cash

      Aladdin Wealth builds and analyses portfolios. It does not net orders or pool client cash, and its subscription price, often sized on the value of positions (10-K), is not comparable to a percentage of client assets.

      Public demand for custom portfolios: Aperio approaching $200bn (Q2-2026 call); $308bn of model portfolios on 31 Mar 2026, of which $87bn custom. H20-BlackRock (Precision against Core fees in the Q3-2026 supplement): not testable, no such lines found.

      Sources: BlackRock 10-K (basis of Aladdin fees); Q2-2026 earnings call, 22 Jul 2026 (Aperio approaching $200bn); BlackRock public figures at 31 Mar 2026 (model portfolios); Q3-2026 supplement (H20-BlackRock).

      Method and sources

      Each test’s question, data, rule and bar were fixed before launch and fingerprinted. Each test was launched once. The official verdict is never replaced.

      Public fingerprints

      SHA-256 hashes of locked rules, data and code: github.com/Samhech/long-tail-portfolio-preregistration. The repository’s results table may lag this page; the project itself is private.

      Tests launched before 16 Oct (up to H16b) have no fingerprint published before their launch; their rules are in the fingerprinted protocol.

      H22 freeze published in commit ec6d4245 · code before launch in commit f0f17b40 · corrected code before relaunch in commit b4a672a3

      Public data

      SEC filings (bank Financial Supplements, 8-K, 10-K and 10-Q; fund N-PORT, N-CEN, N-CSR, tender offers and prospectus fee data; 13F holdings for H22); the Kenneth French data library; public ETF prices; Schwab ETF investor surveys (2023–2025); BlackRock releases, 10-K and Q2-2026 call transcript; the public Robintrack archive.

      Note 15Pre-registration and one launch per testA protocol kept since 25 Sep 2026; code fixes logged as corrections, not new trials

      The question, data, rule and bar of each test were written and fixed before launch, in a protocol kept since 25 Sep 2026 with dated amendments. The bank thresholds were computed before any bank document was read.

      Each test is launched once. Code fixes are logged as corrections, not new trials: step 7 (25 Sep), the bank simulation (26 Sep), a units error in a tool check (27 Sep) and the H22 launch (23 Oct). No verdict changed. Since step 16 every launch follows a dry run on a fictitious panel.

      Note 16Retained readings and independent recomputationDated, labelled before or after launch; Python and R recomputations matched

      The official verdict is never replaced. A more favourable reading is dated, labelled before or after launch, and shown beside it. Nothing is rounded in the thesis’s favour.

      A Python recomputation from the written rules matched every official H17–H21 estimate. Python and R recomputations matched H22’s main estimates; its dry-run counts were checked against the journal, not re-simulated. The bank simulation was rerun with six seed series: +$0.85bn (model output) to +$1.15bn (model output), 55.2% (model output) to 57.7% (model output) of worlds. The official seed gives the lowest lead; the verdict holds on all six.

      Note 17Corrections and incidentsThe step-16 erratum, a late hash, three blindness incidents, one relaunch

      Also logged: the step-16 erratum, the H17–H18 panel fix, the Q4-2026 forecast hash pushed one day late (17 Oct), blindness incidents on 10, 20 and 23 Oct (9 H22 values seen on 23 Oct), and the stopped H22 launch with its single relaunch.

      Note 18What the model does not count, or only assumesNet interest income on client cash, each firm’s real size, client switching

      The net interest income a bank already earns on client cash; each firm’s real size (the model bank holds $500bn); and client switching between banks, which is assumed (25–75% of niche-seeking clients) and measured nowhere.

      Note 19How this page computesThe R model, precomputed in about 37 minutes; 122 of 123 checks match

      All simulator, map and scenario figures come from the R model, precomputed in about 37 minutes on the official grid and on extra cells, then embedded in this page. The page interpolates between grid points and runs no model. 122 of 123 checks against published values match within stated tolerances; the one miss is break-even demand, which interpolation reads as 11.5%, so the page shows the published 12.0%.
